questions.q: State the three conditions of the Second Derivative Test for a critical point \( c \) where \( f'(c)=0 \).
questions.a: Correct answer: (i) If \( f''(c) < 0 \), \( f \) has a local maximum at \( c \). (ii) If \( f''(c) > 0 \), \( f \) has a local minimum at \( c \). (iii) If \( f''(c) = 0 \), the test fails; use the First Derivative Test. A wrong answer (e.g., swapping the inequality signs) reveals the student has memorised the test backwards — they confuse concave down (maximum) with concave up (minimum). This is the single most common sign error in board exams.

questions.q: Explain why the Second Derivative Test fails for \( f(x)=x^4 \) at \( x=0 \), and determine the nature of the critical point using the First Derivative Test.
questions.a: Correct answer: \( f'(x)=4x^3 \), so \( f'(0)=0 \). \( f''(x)=12x^2 \), so \( f''(0)=0 \) → test fails. For \( x<0 \), \( f'(x)<0 \) (decreasing); for \( x>0 \), \( f'(x)>0 \) (increasing). Sign changes from negative to positive → local minimum at \( x=0 \). A wrong answer that stops at "test fails" without applying the First Derivative Test shows the student treats the failure as a dead end rather than a signal to switch methods — a habit that costs marks in multi-step JEE problems.

questions.q: Find the local maxima and minima of \( f(x)=2x^3-9x^2+12x+1 \) using the Second Derivative Test. Show all steps.
questions.a:
Correct answer:
\( f'(x)=6x^2-18x+12=6(x-1)(x-2) \). Critical points: \( x=1, 2 \).
\( f''(x)=12x-18 \).
\( f''(1)=12-18=-6 < 0 \) → local maximum at \( x=1 \), value \( f(1)=6 \).
\( f''(2)=24-18=6 > 0 \) → local minimum at \( x=2 \), value \( f(2)=5 \).
A wrong answer where the student writes \( f''(1)=6 \) (forgetting the minus sign) or mis-evaluates \( f(1) \) as 5 reveals algebraic carelessness in substituting into the second derivative or the original function — a frequent source of 1-mark errors in board papers.

questions.q: Compare the First and Second Derivative Tests for the function \( f(x)=x^3-3x+3 \). Which test is more efficient and why?
questions.a: Correct answer: Both work. First Derivative Test requires checking sign of \( f'(x)=3(x-1)(x+1) \) on intervals \( (-\infty,-1), (-1,1), (1,\infty) \) — three test points. Second Derivative Test: \( f''(x)=6x \), evaluate at \( x=-1 \) (negative → max) and \( x=1 \) (positive → min) — only two evaluations. Second Derivative Test is more efficient here because \( f''(x) \) is simpler than sign analysis of \( f'(x) \). A student who claims First Derivative Test is always better fails to recognise that efficiency depends on algebraic complexity — a key judgment skill for competitive exams where time matters.

questions.q: A student solves \( f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+15 \) and writes: "\( f'(x)=3x^2-12x+9=3(x-1)(x-3) \), critical points \( x=1,3 \). \( f''(x)=6x-12 \). \( f''(1)=-6<0 \) → max at \( x=1 \). \( f''(3)=6>0 \) → min at \( x=3 \)." Is the solution fully correct? If not, identify the error.
questions.a: The solution is correct in classification but incomplete: the student did not state the local maximum and minimum *values* \( f(1) \) and \( f(3) \). Board marking scheme requires the values (or at least the points with coordinates). A student who stops at "max at x=1" loses 1 mark per extremum. This tests whether the student understands that "local maximum" means the *value* \( f(c) \), not just the x-coordinate.

questions.q: Construct a cubic polynomial \( f(x) \) that has a critical point at \( x=2 \) where the Second Derivative Test fails, but the First Derivative Test shows a local minimum. Write the polynomial and verify both tests.
questions.a: Example: \( f(x)=(x-2)^4 \) or \( f(x)=x^4-8x^3+24x^2-32x+16 \). Check: \( f'(x)=4(x-2)^3 \), \( f'(2)=0 \). \( f''(x)=12(x-2)^2 \), \( f''(2)=0 \) → test fails. For \( x<2 \), \( f'(x)<0 \); for \( x>2 \), \( f'(x)>0 \) → sign change negative to positive → local minimum at \( x=2 \). A poor answer would give a cubic (degree 3) — but a cubic's second derivative is linear, so \( f''(c)=0 \) implies inflection, not min/max. This reveals the student doesn't connect polynomial degree to the order of the first non-zero derivative.
